criteria.note: The keyword intent — how to spot gluten on a Korean food label — is answered in the opening paragraph with the actual Hangul word to look for, before any framing.
Title is 38 chars (58 with the rendered suffix), description is 153 chars, keyword terms present in both, and the description adds the 4-step framing rather than restating the title.
Headings carry the argument on their own: skimming Step 1–4 plus 'When the label can't answer' and 'Three Korea-specific gluten-label traps' reproduces the whole method and its limits.
Four distinct internal destinations, each placed where the reader would actually want the detour (low-gluten trap, soy sauce, brand-level snack breakdown, pillar guide).

All three FAQ answers are fully established in the body — the 별표 2 wheat-only scope, the voluntary shared-facility line, the 소비자상담실 route, the rice/밀 전분 trap, and every term in the vocabulary table — and each stands alone as a rich result.
There is a genuine failure narrative and a documented self-correction, but nothing is anchored to a named product, store, or date, so the first-hand layer stays concrete-but-thin.
criteria.evidence_quote: Everything about what sits on convenience-store shelves is our own shopping in Seoul — first-hand, but not a survey, and not lab-tested.

criteria.note: Korean terms are given in Hangul with romanisation and English gloss in a scannable table, the 소맥/밀 synonym trap is named, and a prior mistranslation is corrected precisely.
The controlling regulatory claim is linked to the primary MFDS text with a specific clause (별표 2) and a retrieval date, plus an explicit caution that the standard is amended.
The article states explicitly what a clean scan cannot establish, flags the method as non-survey and non-lab-tested, and contains no commercial links to disclose.

findings.quote: The snack that broke me of trusting the allergen line alone was a "rice" cracker: allergen line clean, but 밀 전분 sitting a few items up in the ingredients.
findings.why: This is the article's single strongest first-hand anecdote, but it carries no product name, brand, store, or date — so it reads as a plausible illustration rather than a verifiable observed event. The rest of the experience signal is similarly unanchored ('our own shopping in Seoul', 'the shelves we scan').
findings.fix: Name the actual cracker (brand + flavour), where and roughly when it was bought, and quote the ingredient line as printed. One named failure with a date does more for E-E-A-T than three unnamed ones.

findings.quote: a small core of convenience-store items keeps clearing the scan for us
findings.why: The list that follows is category-level (eggs, whole fruit, plain yogurt) — anyone who has never been in a Korean convenience store could write it. It does not demonstrate the repeated shelf-level scanning the article claims as its method.
findings.fix: Attach at least two named SKUs per bullet (chain + product), with the month scanned, and note one item that changed formulation between scans — that would evidence the 'reformulate without redesigning the package' warning you already make.

findings.quote: **Rice crackers (쌀과자)** — but only *after* you scan, because of the wheat-starch trap above
findings.why: Terminology and regulatory citation are precise throughout, but the product layer is entirely generic — no manufacturer, no ingredient panel reproduced. A reader cannot check any specific product claim against a package.
findings.fix: Add a short worked example: one real package's 원재료명 line transcribed verbatim, with the gluten words highlighted, so a reader can compare it to what they hold.

findings.quote: the MFDS runs a public food database at [식품안전나라](https://www.foodsafetykorea.go.kr)
findings.why: The primary MFDS standard is dated ('retrieved August 2026'), but this second source is linked with no retrieval date or note on coverage limits beyond 'not every product is in it'. Minor inconsistency in an otherwise well-dated sourcing pattern.
findings.fix: Give 식품안전나라 the same treatment as the labeling standard — retrieval date, and the exact database name/path used (e.g. 품목보고 조회) so the reader lands on the right search.

criteria.note: Regulatory claims are linked and dated, shelf claims are explicitly marked as first-hand observation, but a small number of compositional claims (notably 물엿) are asserted flat without source or observation marker.
criteria.evidence_quote: 물엿 is usually corn-derived, but 조청 is traditionally saccharified with 엿기름, so it's a check rather than a pass.

criteria.note: No invented brands, products, or statistics; the MFDS standard, 별표 2, and foodsafetykorea.go.kr are all real and checkable, and the July publication date plus the August 2026 update note and retrieval dates are internally consistent.

A dedicated paragraph separates the regulatory reading from the authors' own Seoul shopping, states it is 'not a survey, and not lab-tested', defines what 'clears the scan' means, and cedes authority to the physical package.

No absolute safety guarantee anywhere; cross-contamination gets its own step, the voluntary nature of shared-facility warnings is called out as the reason absence proves nothing, and celiac is consistently routed to the stricter action rather than folded in with NCGS.

The MFDS standard carries an explicit August 2026 retrieval date with a warning that it is amended regularly, and the reformulation caution tells readers a package that cleared last month can fail this month.

The load-bearing fact is correct — wheat is mandatory on the allergen line while barley and rye are not — and the terms (원재료명, 알레르기 유발물질, 소맥/소맥분, 엿기름 as malted barley, 맥아, 혼합제제) and romanisations are accurate.
Readers get the law.go.kr link to the standard itself, the 식품안전나라 database with its coverage caveat, and a copy-pasteable Korean question plus where to find the 소비자상담실 number on the panel.

findings.quote: 물엿 is usually corn-derived, but 조청 is traditionally saccharified with 엿기름, so it's a check rather than a pass.
findings.why: The compositional claim about 물엿 is neither sourced nor marked as the authors' own observation, unlike the shelf claims elsewhere in the piece, and it leans in the permissive direction — a reader may read 'usually corn-derived' as clearing 물엿 while 조청 gets an explicit 'check'. The harm ceiling is low (starch syrups are widely treated as low-risk), but the asymmetry in hedging is unearned.
findings.fix: Either cite a source for the corn-derived norm or mark it as observation, and give 물엿 the same 'check rather than a pass' treatment as 조청 — e.g. 'commonly corn- or tapioca-derived in our reading, but the label rarely names the source grain, so treat it as unresolved.'

findings.why: Stated as a flat category fact without a source. It holds for the commercial 양조간장/진간장 used in marinades, which is the context here, but not for traditional 한식/조선간장, which is soybean-and-salt. The error direction is over-cautious so no reader eats gluten because of it, but it is an unsourced absolute in an article that is otherwise careful to hedge.
findings.fix: Narrow to the context: 'the marinade uses commercial 양조간장, which is wheat-brewed'. The linked hidden-gluten guide can carry the fuller distinction.
